title: A landscape before the story
paragraphs: To begin a history of Korea with a king would be to arrive extraordinarily late. Long before cities, kingdoms, written records, or even the earliest human camps, the land that would become the Korean Peninsula was shaped through processes working on timescales almost beyond imagination. Mountains were raised and eroded, buried rock was transformed under pressure, rivers cut their passages, and shorelines moved as the earth and the sea changed around them. This is the deep setting for everything that follows.

The peninsula is not a uniform block of land. Its ridges and basins, its contrasting eastern and western coasts, and its intricate relationship with continental northeast Asia created different possibilities for human settlement. In later centuries the same landforms would influence the direction of roads, the locations of capitals, the movement of armies, and the growth of farming communities. Geography never dictated history by itself, but it established a remarkably durable set of opportunities and constraints.

Geological history must also be approached with a different kind of evidence. There are no eyewitnesses and no chronicles for the formation of an ancient mountain belt. Instead, scientists read rock layers, minerals, faults, sediments, and the structures preserved underground. Each is part of a record created without writing. Reading that record is an act of reconstruction: sometimes precise, sometimes provisional, and frequently revised as new measurements become available.
